rashi:a1.1: So that animals will be available: since the gathering time for animal tithe is not until just before the Festivals, people hold on to their animals until that time and do not slaughter them until they tithe them at the gathering time, which is close to the Festival. So animals turn out to be available for the pilgrims to buy, whether for eating or for offerings. And even though we learned, etc.
gershom:a1.1: So that animals will be available for the pilgrims to buy, since after they have tithed them they sell them.
rashi:a2.1: A mitzva: to be tithed, [that is, he wants the animals] to be tithed.
tosafot:a2.1: A person prefers to perform a mitzva with his money: even though before the set time he may tithe, slaughter and sell, since the Sages fixed a time, it is people’s way to wait longer and tithe everything together.
gershom:a2.1: And even though we learned, “Until the gathering time arrives, etc.”: even so, he holds them until the gathering time and tithes them, since a person prefers to perform the mitzva of tithing them and then sell them.
rashi:a3.1: That it renders them untithed like the threshing floor: by rabbinic law, as we said in the mishna: once the gathering time has arrived, one may not sell or slaughter until he tithes.
gershom:a3.1: That it renders them untithed like the threshing floor: like untithed grain, by rabbinic law and not by Torah law.
gershom:a11.1: And if he slaughtered, he is exempt [as the mishna on 57b rules]: since it is not untithed by Torah law.
rashi:a5.1: Peros: like perusa, a piece broken off [that is, a half].
rashi:a5.2: Thirty days: and half of that is fifteen days.
gershom:a4.1: Peras is half: as it says [about] how long one must stay in a house afflicted with leprosy [to become impure]: the time it takes to eat a peras; and that peras is half [a loaf], as we say: half of it for the afflicted house.
rashi:a6.1: And ben Azzai: he too holds that the gathering time is at the peras of the Festival, fifteen days before it, since from the twenty-ninth of Adar to the fourteenth of Nisan is fifteen [days].
rashi:a6.2: Sometimes it falls on the thirtieth day: when Adar is full.
rashi:a6.3: He does not fix a time: [he does not say] which day of Adar he means.
gershom:a5.1: Sometimes the gathering falls on the thirtieth of Adar, when it is full, since there are still fifteen days to Passover, and sometimes it falls on the twenty-ninth of Adar, when it is defective. That is why Rabbi Akiva does not fix a time.
gershom:a6.1: On the twenty-ninth of Adar and on the first of Sivan.
rashi:a7.1: Since they are not many: the animals born from the peras of Passover until that time. That is why he does not move it earlier and tithe fifteen days before the Festival, as for the other Festivals.
rashi:a7.2: For if you say, etc., they are used up: for once they are tithed, all their animals would be sold and eaten.
gershom:a7.1: Why does ben Azzai not give a peras of fifteen days for Shavuot, but only five days? Since those born in the summer are not many, if you say he should tithe earlier, fifteen days before, they will be used up before the Festival, being eaten, and there will be no animals available for the pilgrims on Shavuot.
rashi:a8.1: By themselves: and not with those born before Elul. So if he were to wait and not tithe until the last day of Elul, which is the peras of the Festival, fifteen days before, he would come to mix those of Elul and those of Av together, and tithe from the new for the old. Therefore he moves it earlier and tithes the summer’s animals on the last day of Av, and not before, since as long as we can bring it close to the Festival, so that they are not used up beforehand, we do so.
gershom:a8.1: Ben Azzai follows his own reasoning: as he says below in the mishna, those of Elul are tithed by themselves.
rashi:a9.1: On the thirtieth day: of Av.
rashi:a9.2: And we require a distinction: granted, one cannot say that he would come to tithe those of Elul and those of Av together, since those of Elul are still too young [to be tithed], as it is still only the first day of Elul. Still, we must make a distinction, so that people will not come to tithe today and tomorrow, new and old together, the new of Elul with the old of Av. Therefore those of Av are not tithed in the new month of Elul at all, not even on its first day.
gershom:a9.1: Sometimes Av is defective: and the thirtieth day is the New Moon of Elul. If we tithed them on the thirtieth day, there would be no distinction between new and old, since by then it is already the time for tithing the new.
rashi:a10.1: In accordance with Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, who says: the halakhot of Passover [are studied] two weeks before, and at that time too we tithe. These Tannaim do not hold of the peras [of fifteen days].
gershom:a10.1: Who says: two weeks, which are fourteen days before Passover.
rashi:a12.1: On the first of Tishrei, etc.: that is why he cannot push the tithing later than the last day of Elul, since we require a distinction between new and old. In tractate Rosh HaShana (8a) the reasoning of Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon, and the reasoning of Rabbi Meir, are explained.
rashi:a13.1: Sakreta: (Rashi adds an Old French gloss), with which they paint the tenth.
tosafot:a13.1: In brief: Tosafot ask why the Gemara gives the red paint as the reason one cannot tithe on a Festival, rather than the rule that one may not consecrate anything on a Festival. They answer that consecrating on a Festival is itself forbidden only by rabbinic decree (Beitza 36b, where riding an animal is forbidden lest one cut a branch), so forbidding [tithing] on its account would be a decree upon a decree. Further, one may even consecrate on a Festival for the festive peace offerings, as one may consecrate one’s Paschal offering on Shabbat and one’s festival offering on the Festival (Shabbat 148b). They object that this permission covers only obligations that have a fixed time, and it is not reasonable that animal tithe should count as such because it can serve as festive peace offerings, for then vow and gift offerings would too, since one fulfills the festive peace offering with them (Ḥagiga 7b); and in any case these answers seem not to apply here, since the Festival in question is Rosh HaShana. They conclude: since the tenth becomes sacred by itself, even if he did not call it the tenth, the prohibition of consecrating on a Festival does not apply to such a consecration. Open on Sefaria for the full text.
rashi:a14.1: Since these say so: Rabbi Meir says on the first of Elul, and Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon say on the first of Tishrei. I do not know whom the halakha follows; therefore those of Elul, etc.
gershom:a12.1: Since these say so: Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon say the first of Tishrei is the new year for animal tithe, and Rabbi Meir says the first of Elul. That is why I say that those of Elul are tithed by themselves, out of doubt, since we do not know whom [the halakha] follows, etc.
rashi:a15.1: Except for this bald one: that is Rabbi Akiva. And where we read throughout the Talmud “Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korḥa” [son of the bald one], that is Rabbi Akiva’s son, as we read there (Shevuot 6a): “Rabbi Yehoshua, the son of Rabbi Akiva, said to Rabbi Akiva.” Evidently ben Azzai was a great sage who knew how to discern which reasoning is sound, and so here too he could have grasped their reasoning [and seen] which is more reasonable.
tosafot:a15.1: In brief: Rashi explains that “this bald one” is Rabbi Akiva and that Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korḥa is Rabbi Akiva’s son. Tosafot object: why would ben Azzai avoid Rabbi Akiva’s name and call him by a term of disgrace, as in “Go up, baldhead” (II Kings 2:23) and “From here to the bald man, how far?” (Shabbat 152a)? And the dates do not fit: in Megilla 28a Rabbi [Yehuda HaNasi] asked Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korḥa how he merited long life, and he blessed him that he reach half his years. Rabbi Akiva married Kalba Savua’s daughter at forty, studied forty years and led Israel forty years (Sifrei: he lived 120 years), and Rabbi was born on the day Rabbi Akiva died (Kiddushin 72a). So even if Rabbi Yehoshua was born in the first year of that marriage, he was eighty when Rabbi was born, and at least 140 when he blessed him, since half his years would be no blessing if it were less than seventy, the ordinary lifespan (Psalms 90:10). Rabbi would then have been sixty, and the blessing would have given him only ten years; what blessing is that? And it seems more likely that he was not born until Rabbi Akiva had spent his twelve and twelve years in the study house, in which case Rabbi would already have passed half those years. Rabbeinu Nissim explains that the bald one is Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya, who the Jerusalem Talmud says was bald; Rabbeinu Tam explains Korḥa as a man’s name. Open on Sefaria for the full text.
gershom:a13.1: Like garlic peel, which is light [and worthless].
gershom:a14.1: Except for this bald one: that is Rabbi Akiva, for Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korḥa is the son of Rabbi Akiva, as we read there (Shevuot 6a): “Rabbi Yehoshua, the son of Rabbi Akiva, said to Rabbi Akiva.” [The note ends with an abbreviation, למ״ה, whose meaning is unclear.]
rashi:a16.1: They said it by tradition: Rabbi Meir, and Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon, all said their statements by tradition, from Haggai, Zechariah and Malachi. That is why ben Azzai did not want to rely on his own [reasoning] and fix the halakha by his own decision.
tosafot:a16.1: From Haggai, Zechariah and Malachi: Rashi explains that since it is prophecy, it is like a halakha without a reason, and one cannot establish by reasoning which of them is primary. But it should not have mentioned prophecy, since a prophet may not introduce anything new from now on; it should rather have said: “They had it as a received halakha.” [Yet the same phrase appears] in chapter Kohen Gadol (Nazir 53a), about a quarter-kav of bones and a half-log of blood: “They said it by tradition, from Haggai, Zechariah and Malachi.” There is a difficulty, however, from what is expounded in the first chapter of Rosh HaShana (8a): “You shall tithe” juxtaposes animal tithe to grain tithe; Rabbi Meir holds the first of Elul, for just as grain tithe is tithed close to its completion, etc.; Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon hold that just as grain tithe’s new year is Tishrei, etc. [So they do have reasons.] One may answer: even so, since these expositions were themselves a tradition from Haggai, Zechariah and Malachi, he could not determine which was primary.
gershom:a15.1: They said it from Haggai, Zechariah and Malachi: these Tannaim did, and it is like prophecy, so he could not establish its reasoning.
rashi:a17.1: Five in Tishrei and five in the Av after it: combine, even though there are gathering times in between.
gershom:a16.1: Five in Tishrei and five in the coming Av combine.
gershom:a17.1: Obvious: that according to ben Azzai those of Elul do not combine.
gershom:a18.1: Lest you say that just as years separate, the beginnings of years, since one does not tithe from the new for the old, so gathering times separate, and these five of Tishrei and five of Av, between which there are gathering times for tithe, I might say do not combine. It teaches us that they combine, as we learned: Five, etc.
rashi:b1.1: And he takes one of those of Elul: not that he aims to bring it out as the tenth, since it is written “He shall not inquire” [Leviticus 27:33]. Rather [he takes] as it falls, for example where he counted them lying down or standing, for then it is not possible [so the printed text] to aim that one of those of Elul be the tenth; whereas if he passed them through the opening under the rod, he would not know when [one of Elul] comes out at the head of the ten. And so we say below: lying down or standing, these are tithed.
rashi:b1.2: And those of Av are exempt: since there are only five from that year.
tosafot:b1.1: And he takes one of those of Elul: the prohibition of “He shall not inquire” does not apply here, as it did to bringing out a blemished animal at the head of the ten, at the beginning of our chapter (53b).
rashi:b2.1: What are you saying, let them combine: those five of Tishrei, with another gathering, with those born later in that same year, so that they combine with them at the peras of Passover. That is not possible, since the Merciful One said that a definite tenth shall be sacred, and not an uncertain one, as here, where perhaps these five of Tishrei were already exempted by the one he took from those of Elul, if Elul is the new year.
gershom:b1.1: What are you saying, let them combine with another gathering? Those five that we said are exempt: the Merciful One said a definite tenth, one that never entered the pen until now, and not an uncertain one, for perhaps the tenth that comes out is one of those five that already entered a gathering, which are uncertain, perhaps of this year and perhaps of last year.
rashi:b3.1: Obvious: that he takes from those of Elul. For if he took from those of Av, it would not be a tenth, since perhaps Elul is the new year, and there are only five from the past year, and they are not subject to tithe at all; and if from those of Tishrei, for the ten of Av and Elul, perhaps Tishrei is the new year, and those five likewise are not subject to tithe; and moreover, those ten of Av and Elul would not be tithed.
rashi:b3.2: To take from these: those of Av and of Tishrei.
gershom:b2.1: Obvious: that according to ben Azzai he must take one of those of Elul. What is Rava teaching us?
gershom:b3.1: Lest you say: let us decree lest he come to take from those that are not of Elul. It teaches us that there is no concern, since he can make those of Elul lie down or stand so that they are recognizable to him, and he can count them that way and will not come to take from the others.
rashi:b4.1: Mishna. To emerge together: for if they emerged together, the ninth and the tenth would be spoiled, as below.
rashi:b5.1: And took ten: that is, he did not count them one, two, three, but each time took ten at once, and from each ten took one as tithe. That is not tithe, since he must count them so that the tenth in the count is sacred.
rashi:b5.2: The reason of Rabbi Yosei is explained in the Gemara.
rashi:b5.3: From the counted: from those that have already passed through the opening under the rod, even though they are not yet tithed; for example, he counted, and one of them went back and jumped into the pen. The counted are exempt by “the fitting count,” as explained in the Gemara, and since it is not known which one is exempt, all those in the pen are exempt.
rashi:b5.4: From the tithed: from the tithe animals themselves.
gershom:b4.1: One of the counted jumped into them: into those in the pen that have not yet been counted; all of them are exempt. Those from one to nine that came out before the tenth came out are called “counted,” and the counted are exempt even if the tenth died in the pen, because of the fitting count: at the time they came out the tenth was still alive and fit to complete the count. Likewise, wherever enough remains in the pen to complete the count of those that came out, those that came out are called “the fitting count.” So when one of the counted jumped into them, all are exempt, since the counted that came out were exempted by the fitting count, and once it jumped in among them, all of them are possibly counted.
gershom:b5.1: From the tithed into them: it refers to the tithe animal itself. All of them must graze, since each of them is possibly the tithe.
rashi:b8.1: Gemara. An orphan: whose mother died before it was born. Now, if they threw a vegetable, the orphan, which is exempt, would also come out. And even though there is an orphan that is obligated, for example one that was born and then its mother died, and that one would come out only by means of a vegetable, still, by standing the mothers of these outside he will have a reminder, and remember that an orphan and a purchased animal are not subject to tithe.
gershom:b6.1: A decree on account of a purchased animal and an orphan: that is why he stands their mothers outside, to make known that there are no purchased animals or orphans there. And their mothers are outside because they are already tithed.
rashi:b9.1: A tereifa does not pass: for example, its legs were broken from the knee joint upward and it cannot walk.
rashi:b10.1: This is the reading: “One might have thought: If he had one hundred, etc.”
gershom:b7.1: And this is not the tenth: since he did not count them.
rashi:b11.1: Two terumot: even though this verse, “your teruma,” is written only about teruma of the tithe, we derive that it also speaks of the great teruma from “as the grain of the threshing floor,” that is, like the great teruma that an Israelite takes from his threshing floor. So teruma of the tithe is juxtaposed to the great teruma for this matter: just as the great teruma, etc.
rashi:b12.1: By estimate: he estimates in his mind that this pile holds so much, and takes teruma according to his estimate.
rashi:b12.2: By thought: he thinks [and says]: “The two log that I am going to separate are teruma,” as we say (Demai 7:4) about one who buys wine from the Samaritans. It is called thought because he does not count them out. Alternatively: he sets his eyes on one side [of the pile] and eats from the other side. Both estimate and thought we derive from “shall be reckoned [ve-neḥshav].”
tosafot:b12.1: In brief: Tosafot note that by Torah law estimate has no place in the great teruma, since one grain exempts the whole pile and the Torah gave it no measure (“the first of your grain,” Deuteronomy 18:4); it applies because teruma of the tithe has a written measure (“a tithe of the tithe,” Numbers 18:26) and the Sages set a measure for the great teruma. Teruma of the tithe cannot be satisfied with one grain on the strength of this juxtaposition, but deliberately adding seems to work: the point is that the great teruma is taken by estimate as a mitzva, so that one gives generously (Terumot 1:7: not by measure, weight or number). They cite readings in the Tosefta and Rabbeinu Tam (“only by estimate and by thought”), the Jerusalem Talmud (Terumot 1), and Menaḥot 55a, where the baraita ends “just as the great teruma is with a generous eye” and Abba Elazar ben Gomel allows counting figs and measuring dried figs for the sake of generosity. They ask from Gittin 30b, where a householder who owed a Levite an unspecified tithe is suspected of not having separated its teruma, though by Abba Elazar ben Gomel he could have done so by estimate; they answer that a householder need not be generous with others’ property and should avoid the complaints of priest and Levite if his estimate errs. They ask from Terumot 4:6 (“one who counts is praiseworthy, one who measures more so”) and the Jerusalem Talmud there, and conclude that for Abba Elazar ben Gomel estimate is valid, not necessarily the preferred way; or that the Rabbis agree estimate is valid but not a mitzva. They ask how estimate is not “adding to tithes,” answer that an honest estimate is not adding, and note from Menaḥot 54b that Abba Elazar ben Gomel allows estimate even for first tithe. Finally they ask why Rabbi Yosei, son of Rabbi Yehuda, must rely on Abba Elazar ben Gomel rather than simply on the juxtaposition of animal tithe to grain tithe; after rejecting one answer, they explain that the animals brought into the pen are usually not equal, so Rabbi Yosei needs a view that allows estimate without concern for over-tithing. They end with Menaḥot 54b on Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Yosei’s father, who took ten dried figs from the corner for ninety in the basket. Open on Sefaria for the full text.
gershom:b8.1: “And your teruma shall be reckoned to you as the grain of the threshing floor”: the verse speaks of two terumot, for the verse juxtaposes teruma of the tithe to the teruma of the threshing floor, which is “as the grain of the threshing floor.” Just as the great teruma is taken by estimate and by thought, in that one need not count up to a hundred and take two, as it says: he sets his eyes on one side and eats from the other side; and as we say: “The two log that I am going to separate are teruma.”
